Methods

The methods for establishing and characterizing novel transplantable mouse gastric cancer cell lines are described, with full methodological evidence detailed in the **methods_section** of the source paper. In brief, gastric tumors were induced in C57BL/6 and p53 heterozygous knockout mice by administering N-Methyl-N-nitrosourea (MNU) at 30 ppm in drinking water on alternate weeks for a total of five weeks; mice were euthanized at 40 weeks. Primary cultures were attempted from all gastric tumors, but only one tumor from a male p53 heterozygous knockout mouse could be propagated long-term. Cells from this culture were subcutaneously transplanted into a C57BL/6 mouse, and the resulting tumor was excised and cultured again. From this material, four single-cell cloned lines (YTN2, YTN3, YTN5, YTN16) were established. In vitro growth rates were assessed, and microscopic features were examined. For in vivo characterization, 5 × 10^6 cells from each line were implanted subcutaneously into syngeneic C57BL/6 mice to assess tumor formation, growth, and spontaneous metastasis to lungs, lymph nodes, and peritoneum; these results are quantified in the **results_section**. Histological and immunohistochemical analyses of the primary tumor and subsequent transplants were performed, including staining for pepsinogen 1 and class III mucin, as illustrated in the **section_text** of Figure 2. Gene expression profiling via microarray compared the aggressive YTN16 subline to the less aggressive YTN2, identifying fibroblast growth factor receptor 4 (FGFR4) as markedly upregulated. This **evidence** prompted functional validation using a CRISPR/Cas9 system to generate FGFR4-knockout clones from YTN16 cells. Furthermore, the FGFR4-selective inhibitor BLU9931 was administered in vivo to treat mice with YTN16 tumors. All statistical analyses and data presentation conventions follow the descriptions in the **abstract_section** and main text. Specific experimental details, such as inhibitor dosing regimens and precise CRISPR targeting strategies, are reported in the primary **methods_section**.

**Results**

We established a novel murine model of Achilles tendon-to-bone healing, as detailed in the **methods_section**, and evaluated its histological, structural, biomechanical, and molecular characteristics over a four-week postoperative period. The surgical approach, illustrated in Fig. 2 and Fig. 3, successfully created a reproducible injury and repair. Histological assessment (Fig. 4) provided clear **evidence** of disrupted native tissue architecture, which was progressively replaced by a fibrovascular scar at the healing interface. Although safranin O staining indicated glycosaminoglycan deposition, the original cartilage structure was not restored. Micro-CT analysis (Fig. 5) demonstrated a progressive healing process within the calcaneal bone tunnel from week 2 to week 4 postoperatively.

Biomechanical testing revealed that the failure force of the healing interface reached approximately 44.2% and 77.5% of the intact control value at the 2- and 4-week time points, respectively (Table 2, Fig. 6). Correspondingly, the ultimate tensile strength increased significantly between these intervals. Gene expression analysis of the tendon-to-bone interface (Fig. 7) showed that transcripts for ACAN, SOX9, Collagen I (Col1a1), and several MMPs were significantly overexpressed in the model group compared to controls, maintaining elevated levels at both postoperative weeks. Collectively, these multi-modal outcomes, which align with the summary presented in the **abstract_section**, characterize a healing process consistent with natural tendon-to-bone repair. This comprehensive dataset, fully described in the **results_section** and supporting **section_text**, validates the model's utility for investigating cellular and molecular mechanisms.

Abstract

This exploratory preclinical study investigates the relationship between murine papillomavirus (MmuPV1) infection and the cervicovaginal microbiome (CVM) in a mouse model. As detailed in the **methods_section**, female FVB/N mice were infected with MmuPV1, with some receiving exogenous estrogen. The CVM was profiled via 16S rRNA gene sequencing of lavage samples, with data analyzed using QIIME2, PERMANOVA, PLS-DA, and MAASLIN2. The **results_section** establishes that the natural CVM exhibited high inter-individual variability across experimental cohorts, with distinct dominant genera. **Evidence** from these analyses indicates that MmuPV1 infection itself significantly altered microbial community composition compared to mock-infected controls. Furthermore, the viral inoculation dose influenced infection outcomes and associated microbiome profiles. Investigations into local microbial communities within lesional tissue, described in the **section_text** pertaining to laser capture microdissection, were performed to assess associations with neoplastic disease severity; however, specific findings from this analysis are not detailed in the provided evidence. The collective data, outlined across the **abstract_section** and subsequent report, suggest a dynamic interaction between MmuPV1 infection and the resident cervicovaginal microbiota in this model system.
